summary: A quiet weekend: Ottawa defends its budget as critics question who it helps, and Ontario teachers have begun voting on whether to authorize strikes.
body: It was a quiet weekend in Canadian politics, with the budget debate continuing. On CTV's Question Period, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said "deficits are lower, that's a fact", pointing out that last year's came in $27.5 billion below the spring forecast because revenue was higher than expected.[^1] The deficit is still projected at over $62 billion next year and above $50 billion a year through 2030, and interest on the debt will cost more than federal health transfers to the provinces.[^1] Champagne says about two-thirds of the new measures aim to grow the economy: "you're not going to borrow for groceries."[^1]

Critics see it differently. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says debt interest "does not buy a single doctor", and NDP Leader Avi Lewis calls the budget a gift to corporations.[^1] An analysis in The Hub finds program spending rises $44 billion, or about 9%, next year.[^2] For young people, a Financial Post review finds the budget leans toward older Canadians, though a larger benefit for low-income workers and changes to first-time buyers' mortgage rules may help younger people.[^3]

Closer to the classroom: Ontario's education unions are holding strike votes this month. Public high-school teachers (OSSTF) began voting on Nov 6, and elementary teachers (ETFO) start on Nov 9, with Catholic and French-language teachers and education workers to follow by Nov 18.[^4][^5] Contracts expired on Aug 31, and talks are stuck on the province's push to bargain more issues centrally.[^5] A "yes" vote does not mean an immediate strike; several legal steps would come first.[^4]
differences: The government calls most new spending investment that will grow the economy; Conservatives say the issue is how much is spent, and the NDP doubts benefits will reach ordinary people.[^1] Outlets total the budget's new measures differently, from about $142 billion to $151 billion, depending on what they count.[^1]
